title: Primary Function of the Rotor Shaft
learningObjectives: Identify the rotor shaft's role in the turbine system.
student: State the primary structural and mechanical function of the rotor shaft.
instructor: The rotor shaft transmits torque from the turbine stages to the connected drivetrain while maintaining acceptable torsional strength and stiffness.

title: Blade-Generated Torsional Loading
learningObjectives: Connect blade loading to a varying internal torque.
student: Explain how the turbine blade stages load the shaft in the base model.
instructor: The blade stages apply torque about the shaft axis. Their cumulative effect makes the internal torque resultant vary continuously along C-D rather than remain constant between isolated point loads.

title: Supports and Rotational Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Distinguish radial support from rotational restraint.
student: Identify supports A, B, and C and state what each prevents.
instructor: Journal bearings A and B prevent radial translation but allow shaft-axis rotation, so they provide no torsional reaction in the ideal model. Section C is fixed against rotation, so θ(C) = 0 and a reaction torque develops there.

title: Torsional Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace torque transfer from the blades to the restraint.
student: Trace the torsional load path through the turbine rotor.
instructor: Steam forces act on the blades; blade hubs transfer torque into the rotor; the shaft carries cumulative internal torque toward restrained section C; and the fixed connection supplies the balancing reaction torque.

title: Expected Critical Location
learningObjectives: Predict the location of maximum torsional stress.
student: Before calculating, predict where the maximum torsional shear stress will occur and explain why.
instructor: Maximum stress occurs where the magnitude of internal torque is largest and at the shaft's outer surface. For the stated linear internal-torque model, the critical cross section is D.

title: Governing Mechanical Responses
learningObjectives: Identify the responses included in the base problem.
student: Identify the mechanical responses central to this problem and list important responses outside the base model.
instructor: The base responses are torsional strength, represented by maximum shear stress, and torsional stiffness, represented by relative angle of twist. Bearing stresses, blade stresses, bending, fatigue, vibration, and thermal behavior are outside the base model.

title: Key Geometry and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Explain how diameter, length, and modulus affect torsional response.
student: Identify the key geometric and material parameters and describe how they affect stress or twist.
instructor: Shaft diameter d controls J proportional to d4, twist proportional to 1/d4, and stress proportional to 1/d3. Loaded length L affects twist linearly. Shear modulus G affects twist but not elastic stress for prescribed torque.

title: Student-Generated Turbine-Shaft Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a varying-torque shaft model before viewing the reference figure.
student: Before using the reference figure, create a simplified shaft model showing A, B, fixed section C, section D, coordinate x measured from C, and the linearly varying internal torque T(x). Include a circular cross section with diameter d.
instructor: A valid model shows a prismatic circular shaft with θ(C) = 0, ideal torque-free journal bearings at A and B, and T(x) = TDx/L for 0 ≤ x ≤ L.
gradingNotes: Students should attempt the model before seeing the instructor idealization.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the turbine-shaft model.
student: State the assumptions required for the base mechanics model.
instructor: Assume a uniform solid circular shaft, homogeneous isotropic linear-elastic material, Saint-Venant torsion, small twist, constant G and d, ideal bearings that transmit no shaft-axis torque, and a perfectly fixed section C. Neglect blade size, local stress concentrations, bending, dynamics, thermal effects, and fatigue.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
student: Outline the calculation sequence before substituting numbers.
instructor: Define T(x); determine the reaction torque at C; construct the internal-torque diagram; compute J; integrate T(x)/(JG) for twist; evaluate Tc/J for stress; and interpret the governing section and parameter sensitivity.

title: Torsional Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: State the boundary conditions used in the torsion solution.
student: State the torsional boundary conditions at A, B, and C.
instructor: At fixed section C, θ(C) = 0. Ideal journal bearings A and B permit rotation and supply no reaction torque about the shaft axis. Their radial reactions are outside the torsion-only model.

title: Fixed-Section Reaction Torque
student: Identify the unknown torsional reaction at C and determine its magnitude and sense.
instructor: The fixed section supplies a reaction torque of magnitude {{turbine_reaction_lbft}} lb·ft, opposite the sense of the blade-region torque. Bearings A and B supply no shaft-axis reaction torque.

title: Internal Torque Function and Diagram
learningObjectives: Define and graph a linearly varying internal torque resultant.
student: Define the internal torque along C-D and construct its diagram. Clearly distinguish an internal torque resultant from a torque intensity per unit length.
instructor:
With x measured from C, T(x) = TDx/L for 0 ≤ x ≤ L. The diagram is triangular, increasing from zero at C to TD at D. The area-average internal torque is {{turbine_average_torque_lbft}} lb·ft.

Here T(x) has torque units; it is not a distributed intensity w(x) with torque-per-length units.
commonMistakes: Do not integrate the stated T(x) once more as though it were a torque intensity.

title: Polar Moment of Inertia
learningObjectives: Calculate the polar moment for a solid circular shaft.
student: Determine the polar moment of inertia J for the assigned solid shaft.

title: Relative Angle of Twist at D
learningObjectives: Integrate a varying internal torque to determine twist.
student: Determine the angle of twist at D relative to C. Show the integral and use consistent inch-pound units.

title: Absolute Maximum Torsional Shear Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate maximum shaft stress and locate it physically.
student: Determine the absolute maximum torsional shear stress and identify its location.
instructor: The largest |T| occurs at D. Therefore τmax = TD(d/2)/J = {{turbine_tau_psi}} psi = {{turbine_tau_ksi}} ksi. It occurs at the outer surface of section D.

title: Torsional Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Compare how design variables affect stress and twist.
student: Explain which design variable most effectively reduces both twist and stress. Compare the effects of increasing diameter, increasing shear modulus, and reducing loaded length.
instructor: Increasing diameter is most effective because J scales with d4, twist scales with 1/d4, and maximum stress scales with 1/d3. Increasing G reduces twist but not stress for prescribed torque. Reducing L reduces twist but not maximum stress at D.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Make a bounded recommendation from the torsion results.
student: Provide a limited engineering recommendation based on the torsion model and identify the checks needed before final turbine-shaft approval.
instructor:
{{turbine_recommendation}}

Final design must verify the intended loading interpretation and include bending, combined stress, fatigue, stress concentrations, blade and rotor dynamics, vibration, thermal gradients, bearings, and project-specific stress and twist limits.
gradingNotes: Students should not claim full rotor safety without allowable limits and the omitted coupled analyses.
